body.text: In 1992, Chief Petty Officer Anita van der Meer made a call that would shape the future for countless serving and future ADF personnel.
She stood accused of being in a same-sex relationship while serving in the navy, which at the time was banned and punishable with dismissal.
Former ADF members have spoken of "witch-hunts" throughout the 1980s, as the Defence Force searched for gay, lesbian and bisexual personnel.
Chief Petty Officer van der Meer says she was not in a relationship with anyone at the time.
Rather than argue, she decided to challenge what she saw as an unjust rule and take her case to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Commission.
"All I wanted to do was serve my country," she said.

"So why should my personal life, which, as I said, I wasn't in a same-sex relationship, I wasn't in a relationship at all, I'd just joined the Defence Force, and all I wanted to do was serve my country.
"And whether I was straight, gay, or whatever, it shouldn't have anything to do with me serving in the Defence Force."
The case was successful, and later that year the federal government would drop the ban and allow gay and lesbian members of the ADF to serve openly.
The change brought consequences not just for those already serving in the ADF, but for future recruits considering a career in the military.
"There was an immediate effect," she said.
"I mean, it was still hard for Defence people to come through because [change] can't happen overnight.
"So it has taken a few years, and we still aren't fully there yet."
She said hearing a formal apology was an enormous moment.
"Very, very emotional. A long time coming," she said.
A long-awaited apology

Anita van der Meer was in the gallery of the House of Representatives on Wednesday, as Defence Minister Richard Marles formally apologised on behalf of the government and the chief of the Defence Force.
"I say to every single individual harmed by these policies and practices: for the surveillance, and the fear you lived under, we are sorry," he said.
"For the interrogations, and for being asked to betray your mates, we are sorry. For the careers ended and the promises wasted, we are sorry.
"For discharge papers that told lies about your service, we are sorry. For the years you felt unwelcome amongst your fellow veterans, we are sorry."
Chief Petty Officer van der Meer joined other LGBTQIA+ members and veterans in laying a wreath at the Australian War Memorial yesterday afternoon, during the daily Last Post Ceremony.
She will retire in a fortnight, after a 37-year career in the navy.
The apology caps a long journey for LGBTQIA+ personnel and veterans looking for equal status within ADF ranks.
Until 1992, the official policy of the ADF was that "homosexual behaviour is not accepted or condoned".
Defence personnel found to be in same-sex relationships would have their service terminated, and many did.
On November 23, 1992, the Keating government resolved to drop the ban on lesbian, gay, and bisexual service.
In 2005, recognition was provided to same-sex partners of ADF personnel for the first time.
It would take another five years, in 2010, before restrictions on transgender personnel transitioning while serving would be lifted.
And in October this year, Defence began allowing current and former personnel to apply to have historical homosexual convictions removed from their service records.
The government then committed to a formal apology to all those affected by what Defence Minister Richard Marles described as a "shameful chapter" in the ADF's history.
He acknowledged in his speech that long after the service bans were lifted, informal barriers would remain.
"For many who continued to serve after 1992, while the ban was lifted, it was a long time before Defence's culture and attitudes caught up," he said.
"We asked these Australians to defend a fair go. Then we refused them one.
"None of this made our nation safer."
'Witch-hunts'
Former RAAF officer Mick Jansen spent years serving in the Royal Australian Air Force before deciding to tell those he served alongside who he really was.
He spent 40 years in the Air Force, joining when the ban was still in place, then seeing it lifted and watching the cultural change slowly follow. He pays tribute to those who led the way before him.
"It was a really difficult thing to do," he said.
"Even when I came out in 2003, it was still not an easy thing. That was 10-odd years after it became legal; it was still an unusual situation to find myself in.
"And so it really was important to have that visibility from people."
Mr Jansen said he was not subjected to the witch-hunts that were going on at the time, but was aware of them happening around him.

"People would be entrapped. They would be trapped and followed and caught going in and out of gay bars, caught doing things that might have indicated that they were part of the LGBT community," he said.
"They were picked up by the military police, interrogated in ways that we might see in the movies, and couldn't imagine what was happening, but was really happening to them.
"It must have been an incredibly frightening event for them to have known that, and to have lived in an environment where you knew that could happen.
"Knew that you might have been hunted down like that, and then presented with the evidence, and then told to either resign or you were going to get kicked out."
He said it was important to hear the apology for all those who experienced those kinds of investigations.
The shadow minister for defence personnel, Phil Thompson, spoke in parliament on behalf of the Coalition, echoing the government.
"Australians who step forward, willing to lay down their lives for us, were subjected to invasive investigations," he said.
"Had their security clearances stripped or downgraded, and were marched out of the gates on administrative discharges.
"Careers were destroyed or cut short, and lives were shattered. Deep, lasting trauma was inflicted — not by an enemy on the battlefield, but by the very institution they had proudly served.
"Let us call this out for exactly what it was. It was wrong."
Advocacy group Just.Equal Australia is now calling on the government to establish a redress scheme, offering compensation to those who lost careers and income due to the policies of the time.
